options.a: Right client, drug, dose, route, time, and documentation
options.b: Right client by room number and bed, then drug and dose
options.c: Right drug, dose, and route as stated by the off-going nurse
options.d: Right drug and dose by matching the pill color to the last dose

distractorExplanations.b: Room and bed numbers are not acceptable identifiers; two client identifiers (name, DOB) must be checked against the MAR.
distractorExplanations.c: A verbal report from another nurse does not replace checking the MAR/order, and it skips client, time, and documentation checks.
distractorExplanations.d: Pill color varies by manufacturer and is not a verification method; the label is checked against the MAR.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-safe-care-001.explanation: Rights of medication administration reduce errors; use two identifiers. Also check allergies and any required assessment as indicated.

options.a: All four side rails up, call light in reach, and bed in high position
options.b: Call light in reach, nonskid footwear, bed in low position, and clutter-free path
options.c: Call light within reach, bed locked in the high position, and regular cotton socks
options.d: Bed in low position, call light across the room to promote walking

distractorExplanations.a: Four raised rails count as a restraint and increase climb-over falls, and a high bed raises injury risk; the bed stays low.
distractorExplanations.c: The bed should be in the low (not high) position, and ordinary socks are slippery; nonskid footwear is required.
distractorExplanations.d: The call light must be within reach so the client asks for help instead of walking alone, which is a fall risk.

options.a: Applying snugly around the waist over clothing and holding underhand while ambulating
options.b: Applying loosely around the chest under the arms and lifting the client by the belt
options.c: Applying snugly over bare skin at the waist and holding it overhand from the front
options.d: Applying around the waist and using it to lift a fallen client back to the bed alone

distractorExplanations.b: The belt goes snugly around the waist, not loosely at the chest, and it is used to steady balance rather than lift.
distractorExplanations.c: The belt is placed over clothing to protect skin, and the nurse grips it underhand from behind or the side for control.
distractorExplanations.d: A gait belt is not a lifting device for fallen clients; assess first, then use a mechanical lift or team as policy directs.

options.a: Inserting a nasogastric tube for feeding
options.b: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter
options.c: Changing a colostomy appliance
options.d: Collecting a clean-catch urine specimen

distractorExplanations.a: The GI tract is not sterile, so NG tube insertion uses clean technique, unlike urinary catheter insertion.
distractorExplanations.c: A colostomy pouch change involves the GI tract and uses clean technique, not sterile technique.
distractorExplanations.d: A clean-catch (midstream) specimen uses cleansing and a sterile cup but is a clean, not sterile, procedure.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-safe-care-006.explanation: Invasive procedures that enter sterile body cavities require aseptic/sterile technique. Catheter insertion is taught as a sterile procedure.

options.a: Powder-free latex gloves and allergy communication on the chart and band
options.b: Latex-free gloves, while other equipment such as tourniquets may contain latex
options.c: Latex-free gloves/equipment and allergy communication on the chart/band
options.d: Premedication with diphenhydramine so standard latex gloves can be used

distractorExplanations.a: Powder-free latex gloves still contain latex proteins; a latex-allergic client needs latex-free products.
distractorExplanations.b: Latex exposure from tourniquets, catheters, or BP cuffs can still trigger a reaction; all equipment must be latex-free.
distractorExplanations.d: Premedication does not make latex exposure safe; avoidance of latex is the prevention strategy.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-safe-care-007.explanation: Allergy prevention is a safety priority. Follow facility policy for allergy alerts.

options.a: A client with a pain level of 6/10 due for PRN analgesia now
options.b: A client with a blood glucose of 180 mg/dL before lunch
options.c: A client with a temperature of 100.2°F (37.9°C) one day after surgery
options.d: A client with new stridor and difficulty breathing after a procedure

distractorExplanations.a: Pain matters but is not an airway threat; stridor and breathing difficulty come first under ABCs.
distractorExplanations.b: Mild hyperglycemia before a meal is not immediately life-threatening compared with a compromised airway.
distractorExplanations.c: A low-grade fever on postoperative day 1 needs follow-up but ranks below new stridor, an airway emergency.

options.a: Objective, factual, and completed per policy without blaming language
options.b: Objective and factual, with a copy placed in the client's medical record
options.c: Completed only when the client was harmed by the error
options.d: Referenced in the nurse's note as 'incident report filed'

distractorExplanations.b: Incident reports are confidential risk-management documents; they are not filed in or copied into the medical record.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports are completed for near misses and no-harm events too, so system problems are caught before harm occurs.
distractorExplanations.d: The chart documents the event and care given, but it does not mention that an incident report was filed.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-safe-care-009.explanation: Incident reports improve systems; follow facility documentation rules carefully. The report is not part of the medical record narrative.

options.a: One nurse counting and signing, with a second nurse signing later in the shift
options.b: Two authorized nurses verifying discrepancies per policy before end of shift
options.c: An authorized nurse and a UAP counting together at every shift change
options.d: Two nurses verifying, with discrepancies reported at the next weekly audit

distractorExplanations.a: A second signature without witnessing the count is not verification; both nurses count together.
distractorExplanations.c: UAP are not authorized to verify controlled substance counts; two licensed nurses must count.
distractorExplanations.d: Discrepancies are reported and resolved before the end of the shift, not held for a weekly audit.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-safe-care-010.explanation: Controlled substance accountability is a legal safety requirement. This applies when policy requires it.

options.a: Wear an N95 respirator and gloves, and keep the door closed at all times
options.b: Wear gloves, and skip hand hygiene after removal since gloves were worn
options.c: Wear gown and gloves for contact with the client/environment and dedicate equipment
options.d: Wear gown and gloves, and share the BP cuff with the roommate without cleaning

distractorExplanations.a: An N95 and closed door are airborne precautions (e.g., TB); contact precautions require a gown and gloves.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves can have defects and hands become contaminated on removal; hand hygiene is done after taking gloves off.
distractorExplanations.d: Equipment is dedicated to the client or disinfected between clients; sharing an uncleaned cuff spreads MDROs.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-safe-care-011.explanation: Transmission-based precautions prevent MDRO spread; hand hygiene after PPE removal. Dedicate equipment when possible.

options.a: Give it crushed in pudding to ease swallowing, then document the dose as given
options.b: Withhold the dose and document refusal, informing the provider at the next rounds
options.c: Notify the RN, then administer the dose since the provider ordered it
options.d: Explore concerns, educate, withhold as refused, notify the provider/RN, and document

distractorExplanations.a: Hiding medication in food without consent is covert administration and violates the client's right to refuse.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting until the next rounds delays notification; the RN/provider is informed promptly per policy.
distractorExplanations.c: An order does not override a competent client's refusal; the medication cannot be given against their wishes.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-safe-care-012.explanation: Informed refusal is a client right; covert meds without consent are unethical/illegal. Follow facility policy.

options.a: Maintain a closed drainage system and keep the bag below bladder level
options.b: Irrigate the catheter daily with sterile saline to prevent blockage
options.c: Disconnect the tubing to empty and rinse the bag each shift
options.d: Hang the bag on the bed rail at bladder level during transport

distractorExplanations.b: Routine irrigation opens the closed system and is not recommended for CAUTI prevention unless ordered for obstruction.
distractorExplanations.c: Breaking the connection between catheter and tubing introduces bacteria; the bag is emptied through its drain spout.
distractorExplanations.d: The bag must stay below bladder level, including during transport, to prevent backflow into the bladder.

options.a: Initial teaching of a new insulin regimen to a stable client
options.b: Reassessing a client's pain 30 minutes after an opioid dose
options.c: Stable clients’ routine vital signs and hygiene within UAP training
options.d: Routine vital signs on a client with a new oxygen requirement

distractorExplanations.a: Teaching, even for a stable client, requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated to UAP.
distractorExplanations.b: Reassessing pain response after an opioid is an evaluation task that stays with licensed nurses.
distractorExplanations.d: A new oxygen need suggests instability; vital signs on unstable clients are not delegated to UAP.

options.a: Prevent disease before it occurs
options.b: Detect disease early through screening
options.c: Limit disability from an existing disease
options.d: Treat disease once symptoms appear

distractorExplanations.b: Early detection through screening (e.g., mammograms) is secondary prevention, not primary.
distractorExplanations.c: Limiting disability and complications from established disease is tertiary prevention.
distractorExplanations.d: Treating symptomatic disease is treatment or secondary care; primary prevention acts before disease starts.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-00.explanation: Primary = prevention; secondary = screening; tertiary = limit disability. Examples include immunizations and safety education.

options.a: Influenza vaccine every five years and a tetanus booster yearly
options.b: Age-appropriate immunizations such as influenza annually
options.c: Live zoster vaccine annually, plus influenza every other year
options.d: Childhood MMR series repeated, since immunity fades after 60

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps the intervals: influenza vaccine is yearly and Td/Tdap boosters are every 10 years.
distractorExplanations.c: Current zoster vaccine is the two-dose recombinant series, not yearly live vaccine, and influenza is annual.
distractorExplanations.d: Adults born before 1957 are presumed MMR-immune; the childhood series is not routinely repeated at 65.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-00.explanation: LPNs reinforce vaccine education; schedules update—refer to current CDC guidance/provider. Others follow the CDC adult schedule.

options.a: Use SPF 8 or higher, applied once in the morning to last through the day
options.b: Use SPF 30 only on cloudy days, since clouds block most UV rays
options.c: Use broad-spectrum SPF as directed, reapply, and seek shade
options.d: Use broad-spectrum sunscreen and seek sun between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.

distractorExplanations.a: SPF 30 or higher is recommended and must be reapplied about every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating.
distractorExplanations.b: Clouds let most UV through, so sunscreen is needed on clear and cloudy days alike.
distractorExplanations.d: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. is peak UV time, when shade should be sought rather than sun exposure.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-00.explanation: UV protection is skin cancer primary prevention. Seek shade especially during peak UV hours.

options.a: Place infant prone on a firm crib mattress to reduce reflux and choking
options.b: Place infant supine on a firm surface without soft bedding/loose blankets
options.c: Place infant side-lying, propped with a wedge and a light blanket
options.d: Place infant supine on a firm surface with bumper pads for safety

distractorExplanations.a: Prone sleeping raises SIDS risk; healthy infants sleep supine, and back sleeping does not increase choking.
distractorExplanations.c: Side-lying is unstable and lets the infant roll prone; wedges and blankets are suffocation hazards.
distractorExplanations.d: Bumper pads are soft bedding that the AAP advises against because of suffocation and entrapment risk.

options.a: Increases risk of cancer, heart disease, stroke, and respiratory disease
options.b: Mainly harms the lungs, with little effect on heart or stroke risk
options.c: Raises lung cancer risk but lowers blood pressure and stroke risk over time
options.d: Is harmful mainly at more than one pack daily, not light smoking

distractorExplanations.b: Smoking is a major cause of coronary disease and stroke, not just lung disease.
distractorExplanations.c: Nicotine raises blood pressure and smoking increases stroke risk; there is no cardiovascular benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: Even light or intermittent smoking raises cardiovascular and cancer risk; there is no safe level.

options.a: Diagnose growth disorders from a single plotted measurement
options.b: Track patterns of weight/height/head circumference over time
options.c: Compare a child's weight to siblings at the same age
options.d: Set target weights a child should reach by each birthday

distractorExplanations.a: A single point cannot show a pattern; growth charts are interpreted by trends across visits.
distractorExplanations.c: Growth charts compare a child to population reference data and to their own trend, not to siblings.
distractorExplanations.d: Percentile curves describe growth patterns; they are not fixed target weights for each birthday.

options.a: Start at high intensity to build fitness, and push through chest tightness
options.b: Start gradually, and treat chest pain during exercise as normal muscle strain
options.c: Start gradually, get provider clearance if high risk, and stop for chest pain
options.d: Start with daily maximal lifting after clearance, limiting fluids to avoid cramps

distractorExplanations.a: Sedentary clients should start at low-moderate intensity, and chest tightness is a stop-and-report warning sign.
distractorExplanations.b: Chest pain during exertion may signal ischemia and must stop activity, not be dismissed as strain.
distractorExplanations.d: Programs progress gradually rather than maximal lifting, and adequate hydration is encouraged, not restricted.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-01.explanation: Progressive activity with warning-sign education is safer. Also stop for severe dyspnea.

options.a: Unsupervised brushing with toothpaste, plus diluted juice at bedtime
options.b: Fluoride-free toothpaste until age 6 to avoid fluorosis, and juice daily
options.c: Supervised brushing once weekly, with the first dental visit at age 6
options.d: Supervised brushing with fluoride toothpaste and limiting sugary drinks

distractorExplanations.a: Preschoolers need supervised brushing, and bedtime juice (even diluted) bathes teeth in sugar and causes caries.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluoride toothpaste is recommended from the first tooth in age-appropriate amounts; daily juice raises caries risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Brushing is twice daily, not weekly, and the first dental visit is recommended by age 1.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-01.explanation: Early dental habits prevent caries; avoid juice bottles at bedtime. Use an age-appropriate amount of fluoride toothpaste.

options.a: Weight-bearing exercise, calcium/vitamin D per provider, and fall prevention
options.b: Swimming as the main bone-building exercise, plus calcium and vitamin D per provider
options.c: Bedrest when bones ache, high-dose vitamin A, and avoiding dairy
options.d: Weight-bearing exercise, calcium per provider, and removing grab bars

distractorExplanations.b: Swimming is not weight-bearing, so it does little to build bone; walking and resistance exercise are preferred.
distractorExplanations.c: Immobility accelerates bone loss, excess vitamin A may weaken bone, and dairy is a key calcium source.
distractorExplanations.d: Grab bars prevent falls and fractures; removing them increases fracture risk in osteoporosis.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-01.explanation: Bone health + fall risk reduction prevents fractures. Exercise as tolerated.

options.a: Around age 40 for average-risk adults
options.b: Around age 45 for average-risk adults
options.c: Around age 50 for average-risk adults
options.d: Around age 65 for average-risk adults

distractorExplanations.a: Age 40 is the USPSTF start for biennial mammography, not colorectal screening.
distractorExplanations.c: Age 50 was the older USPSTF start; the 2021 update lowered it to 45 for average-risk adults.
distractorExplanations.d: Age 65 is Medicare eligibility, not a screening start; average-risk screening begins at 45.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-01.explanation: Screening ages evolve; nurses teach to follow current guidelines/provider advice (commonly starting mid-40s now). This follows updated USPSTF guidance; confirm with the provider.

options.a: Medical terms with definitions, and asking 'Do you understand?'
options.b: Detailed handouts at a 12th-grade level and one long session
options.c: Plain language, teach-back, and limited key points
options.d: Plain language with many key points covered in one visit

distractorExplanations.a: Yes/no questions like 'Do you understand?' do not confirm learning; teach-back has the client explain in their own words.
distractorExplanations.b: Materials should be written at about a 5th–6th grade level, delivered in short sessions with checks for understanding.
distractorExplanations.d: Covering many points at once overloads clients; limit teaching to a few key points per session.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-health-promo-01.explanation: Teach-back confirms understanding and improves adherence. Provide written materials at an appropriate reading level.

options.a: Ask directly about suicidal ideation and plans and ensure safety
options.b: Offer reassurance that the feeling will pass and redirect to activities
options.c: Avoid the word suicide so the idea is not planted, and observe
options.d: Promise to keep it confidential to build trust, then ask about plans

distractorExplanations.b: False reassurance and redirection close down the conversation and miss suicide risk assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea; avoiding the word is a myth that delays assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Suicide risk cannot be kept secret; the nurse must share it with the team to keep the client safe.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-psychosocial-00.explanation: Direct screening and safety trump avoidance; duty to protect limits confidentiality when harm is imminent. Notify the RN/provider per protocol.

options.a: Putting the client's unstated feelings into words to check understanding
options.b: Repeating the main idea to show listening and encourage clarification
options.c: Summarizing the main points discussed at the end of the session
options.d: Asking the client to explain further what they meant by a statement

distractorExplanations.a: That describes verbalizing the implied, which names feelings the client has not stated, not restating the main idea.
distractorExplanations.c: Summarizing pulls together the key points of a whole conversation, usually at the end, not repeating one statement.
distractorExplanations.d: Asking for more explanation of an unclear statement is clarifying, a different technique from restating.

options.a: Confronting denial about drinking during the first day
options.b: Referral to a 12-step group before discharge planning
options.c: Safety monitoring for withdrawal complications
options.d: Nutrition teaching about thiamine-rich foods

distractorExplanations.a: Confronting denial is not helpful in early detox; physiologic stability comes before psychosocial work.
distractorExplanations.b: 12-step referral is part of later recovery planning; early detox priority is preventing seizures and DTs.
distractorExplanations.d: Thiamine is given early to prevent Wernicke's, but diet teaching waits until withdrawal is medically managed.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-psychosocial-00.explanation: Physiologic withdrawal can be life-threatening; medical stabilization first. Monitor for seizures and DT risk per protocol.

options.a: Calm environment, consistent caregivers, and toileting/pain check
options.b: Reorienting firmly to the date and correcting false beliefs each time
options.c: Group activities with music and TV to keep the client busy at dusk
options.d: PRN sedation and a lap belt as first-line measures at dusk

distractorExplanations.b: Repeated correction and arguing increase agitation in dementia; validation and redirection work better.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiple stimuli at dusk overstimulate clients with sundowning; a calm, low-stimulus setting is preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: Chemical and physical restraints are last resorts after unmet needs and nonpharmacologic measures are addressed.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-psychosocial-00.explanation: Address unmet needs; least restrictive measures first. Offer simple reassurance.

options.a: Intense sadness that eases gradually over the first several months
options.b: Minimal emotional expression initially with later unexpected distress
options.c: Persistent yearning lasting more than 12 months with impairment
options.d: Exaggerated grief with self-destructive behavior soon after the loss

distractorExplanations.a: Intense sadness that gradually eases describes normal (uncomplicated) grief, not delayed grief.
distractorExplanations.c: Persistent yearning beyond 12 months with impairment is prolonged grief disorder, not delayed or inhibited grief.
distractorExplanations.d: Excessive, self-destructive reactions soon after the loss describe exaggerated grief, not delayed grief.

options.a: Distract the client with an activity and recheck at the end of the shift
options.b: Explain that the voices are not real and turn off the television
options.c: Take the command hallucination seriously, assess safety, and report promptly
options.d: Agree to keep the TV off and document the statement in the chart

distractorExplanations.a: Distraction without a safety assessment delays response to a command to self-harm; it needs immediate evaluation.
distractorExplanations.b: Arguing about reality and removing the TV does not assess the command's content or the client's intent to act.
distractorExplanations.d: Documenting without assessing intent or reporting leaves a self-harm command hallucination unaddressed.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-psychosocial-00.explanation: Command hallucinations require urgent safety assessment. Report for evaluation.

options.a: Avoiding detailed information so the client does not worry more
options.b: Giving reassurance that nothing will go wrong during surgery
options.c: Sedating the client before the consent is discussed
options.d: Providing clear procedural information and allowing questions

distractorExplanations.a: Withholding information increases fear of the unknown; clear explanations reduce preoperative anxiety.
distractorExplanations.b: Promising nothing will go wrong is false reassurance and can undermine trust and informed consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent must be obtained before sedation; sedated clients cannot give valid informed consent.

options.a: Privately, with sensitivity, and with knowledge of resources
options.b: With the partner present so the client feels supported
options.c: Only when injuries are visible during the physical exam
options.d: Privately, using a family member as interpreter to ease trust

distractorExplanations.b: Screening is done without the partner present; the partner may be the abuser and silence the client.
distractorExplanations.c: Abuse often leaves no visible injury; routine screening is recommended regardless of physical findings.
distractorExplanations.d: Family members should not interpret abuse screening; use a qualified medical interpreter.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-psychosocial-00.explanation: Screen alone; follow mandatory reporting rules for vulnerable populations/state laws. Know the reporting laws.

options.a: Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis from repeated vomiting
options.b: Electrolyte imbalances and dental/esophageal injury risks
options.c: Weight loss below 85% of ideal as the main risk
options.d: Lanugo and amenorrhea from severe starvation

distractorExplanations.a: Vomiting causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis from loss of potassium and stomach acid, not the reverse.
distractorExplanations.c: Very low body weight is typical of anorexia; clients with bulimia are often at normal weight.
distractorExplanations.d: Lanugo and amenorrhea are classic anorexia nervosa findings, not the main purging risks.

options.a: Applying a cultural guide's beliefs to every client of that group
options.b: Using a bilingual family member as the interpreter to build trust
options.c: Asking about health beliefs/preferences rather than stereotyping
options.d: Treating every client identically so no one is singled out

distractorExplanations.a: Assuming everyone in a group holds the same beliefs is stereotyping; each client is assessed individually.
distractorExplanations.b: Family interpreters compromise accuracy and confidentiality; qualified medical interpreters are used.
distractorExplanations.d: Identical care ignores individual beliefs and preferences; cultural competence adapts care to the person.

options.a: Using rewards and tokens to reinforce desired behaviors on the unit
options.b: Individual sessions exploring unconscious conflicts
options.c: Gradual exposure to feared situations in a safe setting
options.d: Using the therapeutic environment and structured interactions

distractorExplanations.a: Rewards and tokens describe behavior modification (token economy), not milieu therapy.
distractorExplanations.b: Exploring unconscious conflicts is psychodynamic psychotherapy, not use of the therapeutic environment.
distractorExplanations.c: Graduated exposure to feared situations is systematic desensitization used for phobias.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-psychosocial-01.explanation: Psychiatric nursing uses milieu as a treatment tool. The aim is to support recovery.

options.a: Reassure the client that a prosthesis will make life the same as before
options.b: Encourage expression of feelings and involve rehab/support resources
options.c: Delay viewing the site until the client is discharged home
options.d: Focus teaching on stump care and defer feelings to the psychologist

distractorExplanations.a: Promising life will be the same is false reassurance that brushes aside the client's grief over body change.
distractorExplanations.c: Gradual viewing of the site with support helps adjustment; delaying it until discharge worsens body image issues.
distractorExplanations.d: Body image concerns are part of nursing care; the nurse encourages expression rather than deferring it.

options.a: Protect PHI, with no exceptions even when harm to others is threatened
options.b: Share PHI freely with the client's family since they are caregivers
options.c: Protect PHI while explaining limits (harm to self/others, abuse reporting)
options.d: Protect PHI, but disclose any details the client's employer requests

distractorExplanations.a: Duty-to-warn/protect and mandated abuse reporting are legal exceptions to confidentiality.
distractorExplanations.b: Family members need the client's authorization to receive PHI, even when they are caregivers.
distractorExplanations.d: Employers have no right to PHI without the client's authorization.

options.a: Elevate HOB, monitor SpO2/respiratory status, and report changes
options.b: Place flat with legs elevated to reduce edema, and recheck in 4 hours
options.c: Encourage oral fluids to thin secretions and monitor lung sounds
options.d: Hold daily weights and I&O until the crackles resolve

distractorExplanations.b: Lying flat with legs up increases venous return and worsens pulmonary congestion; the HOB is raised.
distractorExplanations.c: Extra fluid worsens overload in heart failure; fluids are usually restricted, not encouraged.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily weights and I&O are key to tracking fluid status and continue during overload.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-001.explanation: Fluid overload threatens gas exchange; follow ABC and orders. Administer ordered diuretics/O2 per plan.

options.a: Glucagon 1 mg IM, then a complex-carbohydrate snack
options.b: 15 g rapid-acting carbohydrate, recheck per protocol
options.c: Protein snack such as peanut butter, then recheck in 1 hour
options.d: A full meal with protein, then recheck at the next scheduled time

distractorExplanations.a: Glucagon is for clients who cannot swallow or are unresponsive; a conscious client takes oral fast carbohydrate.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein and fat slow glucose absorption; fast carbohydrate is given first, with a recheck in 15 minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: A full meal acts too slowly and the recheck is needed in about 15 minutes, not at the next scheduled check.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-002.explanation: Treat low glucose first; unresponsive clients need emergency glucagon/IV dextrose per protocol/RN-provider. This is the 15-15 rule.

options.a: Avoid all vitamin K foods and report bleeding; keep INR appointments
options.b: Keep vitamin K consistent and use ibuprofen rather than acetaminophen
options.c: Keep vitamin K intake consistent and report bleeding/bruising
options.d: Keep vitamin K consistent and double the next dose if one is missed

distractorExplanations.a: Vitamin K intake should be consistent, not eliminated; avoiding it makes INR unstable.
distractorExplanations.b: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen raise bleeding risk with warfarin; acetaminophen is preferred for minor pain.
distractorExplanations.d: Missed warfarin doses are not doubled; clients take the missed dose the same day or follow provider instructions.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-003.explanation: Anticoagulation teaching focuses on consistency, bleeding signs, and interaction awareness. Keep INR appointments.

options.a: Lower the PCA basal rate, recheck vital signs in 30 minutes, and report at shift end
options.b: Let the client sleep since pain is controlled, and recheck RR in 1 hour
options.c: Teach the family to press the PCA button when the client grimaces
options.d: Stop the PCA/opioids, support airway/breathing, stimulate, and notify RN/provider

distractorExplanations.a: RR 6 with poor arousal is an emergency; the opioid is stopped and help called now, not reported at shift end.
distractorExplanations.b: Difficulty arousing with RR 6 is opioid-induced respiratory depression, not restful sleep, and needs action now.
distractorExplanations.c: PCA by proxy is unsafe; only the client presses the button, so sedation limits further dosing.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-004.explanation: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is an emergency. Prepare naloxone as ordered.

options.a: Increase inspiratory volume and strengthen the diaphragm
options.b: Prolong exhalation and prevent airway collapse/air trapping
options.c: Raise CO2 levels to stimulate the respiratory drive
options.d: Shorten exhalation so more oxygen is inhaled per minute

distractorExplanations.a: Strengthening the diaphragm is the goal of diaphragmatic breathing; pursed-lip breathing prolongs exhalation.
distractorExplanations.c: Pursed-lip breathing helps empty trapped air and lower CO2 retention; it does not aim to raise CO2.
distractorExplanations.d: Pursed-lip breathing lengthens exhalation to prevent air trapping; shortening it worsens hyperinflation.

options.a: Mild itching under the cast without neurovascular change
options.b: Warm, pink toes with brisk capillary refill and mild swelling
options.c: Dull ache relieved by elevation and the ordered analgesic
options.d: Increasing pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, paralysis

distractorExplanations.b: Warm, pink toes with brisk refill show adequate perfusion; mild swelling is managed with elevation.
distractorExplanations.c: Pain relieved by elevation and analgesics is expected; compartment syndrome pain is unrelieved and increasing.
distractorExplanations.a: Mild itch can occur.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-008.explanation: Compartment syndrome is limb-threatening—escalate ASAP. These are compartment syndrome signs.

options.a: Facility-required method (often x-ray initially; pH/markings per policy)
options.b: Air bolus auscultation over the epigastrium as the sole check
options.c: Observing for bubbling when the tube end is placed in a cup of water
options.d: Confirming the client can talk clearly and is not coughing after insertion

distractorExplanations.b: Auscultating an air bolus is unreliable and cannot tell gastric from respiratory placement.
distractorExplanations.c: Bubbling in water is an outdated, unreliable test that can mislead in either direction.
distractorExplanations.d: Small-bore tubes can enter the airway with no coughing or voice change, so absence of symptoms proves nothing.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-009.explanation: Misplacement risks aspiration; follow current verification standards. Air auscultation alone is not acceptable.

options.a: Bradycardia, moist mucous membranes, and pale dilute urine output
options.b: Tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, concentrated urine
options.c: Jugular venous distention, weight gain, and peripheral edema
options.d: Tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, and dilute high-volume urine

distractorExplanations.a: Dehydration causes tachycardia, dry membranes, and concentrated urine; these findings suggest normal or excess volume.
distractorExplanations.c: JVD, weight gain, and edema are signs of fluid overload, the opposite of dehydration.
distractorExplanations.d: In dehydration the kidneys conserve water, so urine is concentrated and low in volume, not dilute.

options.a: Thirty to sixty minutes before meals like regular insulin
options.b: At bedtime with a snack to cover overnight glucose levels
options.c: At mealtime / when the tray is present per timing rules
options.d: Once daily at the same time each morning like insulin glargine

distractorExplanations.a: Giving lispro 30–60 minutes early follows regular insulin timing and risks hypoglycemia before the meal.
distractorExplanations.b: Overnight coverage comes from basal insulin; rapid-acting lispro at bedtime risks nocturnal hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.d: Once-daily dosing describes basal insulin such as glargine, not rapid-acting mealtime lispro.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-011.explanation: Match rapid insulin to carbohydrate intake to prevent hypoglycemia. Onset is about 15 minutes.

options.a: Cyanosis of the lips and nail beds
options.b: Bradycardia and hypotension
options.c: Decreased LOC and bradypnea
options.d: Restlessness and tachycardia

distractorExplanations.a: Cyanosis is a late sign of hypoxia; earlier signs are restlessness and tachycardia.
distractorExplanations.b: Bradycardia and hypotension appear late as hypoxia worsens; early on the heart rate rises.
distractorExplanations.c: Decreasing LOC and slowed breathing are late, ominous signs; early hypoxia causes restlessness and tachypnea.

options.a: Stop the transfusion, keep IV line open with NS, and notify provider
options.b: Slow the transfusion rate, give acetaminophen, and recheck in 15 minutes
options.c: Stop the transfusion, flush the blood tubing with D5W, and notify provider
options.d: Finish the unit quickly, then report the symptoms to the provider

distractorExplanations.b: Chills, fever, and back pain may be a hemolytic reaction; the transfusion is stopped, not slowed.
distractorExplanations.c: D5W hemolyzes red cells; the line is kept open with normal saline through new tubing.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuing the transfusion gives more incompatible blood; the reaction requires stopping it immediately.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-013.explanation: Suspect acute hemolytic/febrile reaction—stop blood, maintain access, escalate. Follow transfusion reaction steps per protocol.

options.a: Reposition the client by pulling on the weak arm, which has less pain sensation
options.b: Approach from the intact side, protect the weak side, and use assistive devices
options.c: Place food on the left side of the mouth and offer thin liquids
options.d: Hold the cane in the hand on the weak side and advance the strong leg first

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling on a weak arm can cause shoulder subluxation; reduced sensation increases injury risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Food goes on the unaffected (right) side, and thin liquids raise aspiration risk with dysphagia.
distractorExplanations.d: The cane is held on the strong side and advanced with the weak leg for support.

nclex-pn-readiness-check-physio-014.explanation: Safety and rehab principles guide hemiparesis care; dysphagia screens matter. Use assistive devices per the PT plan.

options.a: Fine hand tremor, polyuria, and a persistent metallic taste in the mouth
options.b: Tinnitus, hearing loss, and rising serum creatinine
options.c: Anorexia, nausea, visual changes (halos), and bradycardia/dysrhythmias
options.d: Hyperactivity with tachycardia and flushing as the classic toxicity pattern

distractorExplanations.a: Fine tremor, polyuria, and metallic taste are typical lithium side effects, not digoxin toxicity.
distractorExplanations.b: Tinnitus and rising creatinine suggest ototoxic/nephrotoxic drugs like aminoglycosides or vancomycin.
distractorExplanations.d: Digoxin toxicity typically causes bradycardia and dysrhythmias with GI and visual symptoms, not hyperactivity.
